clinicalPearls: Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL) is a malignancy of mature B lymphocytes and accounts for ~10% of all lymphomas diagnosed each year; most are classical HL (cHL), with nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL (NLPHL) a distinct second subtype (p.868).

Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells are diagnostic of cHL: large cells with abundant cytoplasm and bilobed and/or multiple nuclei, comprising <1% of tumor cellularity within a surrounding polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, macrophages, plasma cells, fibroblasts, and collagen (p.868-869).

By immunohistochemistry HRS cells are often PAX-5 positive but have low to no expression of other B-cell antigens such as CD19 and CD20; they express CD15 and CD30 in 85% and 100% of cases, respectively (p.868).

Most patients present with nontender palpable lymphadenopathy, typically in the neck, supraclavicular area, and axilla; more than half have mediastinal adenopathy at diagnosis, sometimes as the initial manifestation (p.869).

About one-third of patients present with B symptoms (fevers, night sweats, and/or weight loss); HL can occasionally present as a fever of unknown origin, more common in older patients with mixed-cellularity HL in an abdominal site (p.869).
Pel-Ebstein fever describes a pattern of fevers persisting for days to weeks, followed by afebrile intervals and then recurrence (p.869).
Pain in lymph nodes on alcohol ingestion and severe unexplained itching (pruritus) are recognized unusual manifestations of HL (p.869).

Staging is anatomically based using the Ann Arbor staging system because the disease tends to march from one lymph node group to the next, often contiguous group; staging guides therapy duration and intensity (p.869).
PET/CT is used for staging and is more accurate than bone marrow biopsy for assessing bone marrow involvement, which in cHL tends to be patchy and may be missed on a unilateral marrow biopsy (p.869).
Cure rates now exceed 85%, and the new central challenge in HL care is late therapy-related toxicity, including a high rate of secondary malignancies and cardiovascular disease (p.868).
harrison.pathophysiology: HL is of B-cell origin. The malignant Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells are large bilobed/multinucleate cells that constitute <1% of the tumor mass; the bulk of the tumor is a surrounding polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate, probably a reaction to cytokines produced by the tumor cells. Immunoglobulin genes in the neoplastic cells are rearranged but not expressed. HRS cells interact with their microenvironment via cell-cell contact and elaboration of growth factors and cytokines, producing a cellular milieu that protects them from host immune attack while supporting their proliferation and survival. 97% of HRS cells in cHL harbor genetic aberrations in the PD-L1 locus on chromosome 9p24.1, causing overexpression of PD-L1 (ligand for the inhibitory PD-1 receptor on immune cells), a mechanism for immune evasion that may also contribute to generalized immune suppression in HL patients. An association with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is suggested: monoclonal/oligoclonal EBV-infected cells are found in 20-40% of HL patients, but a definitive etiologic role is not settled. Viral oncogenesis appears greater in HIV-related cHL, where EBV is detectable in nearly all cases (versus only one-third of non-HIV-associated cHL) and HRS cells express EBV latent membrane protein 1 (LMP-1) with episomal, clonal EBV genomes suggesting direct involvement in early lymphomagenesis (p.868-869).
additionalDifferentials: Anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (can mimic HL, especially in older patients)
additionalInvestigations: Adequate biopsy specimen reviewed by an expert hematopathologist (required to establish the diagnosis)
Immunohistochemistry: PAX-5, CD15, CD30 (and CD19/CD20, typically low/absent in cHL)
PET/CT for anatomic staging (more accurate than marrow biopsy for patchy marrow involvement)
Chemistry studies reflecting major organ function, including serum albumin

Careful history (including presence/absence of B symptoms) and physical exam attentive to peripheral nodes, liver, and spleen size; review of comorbidities such as pulmonary disease and congestive heart failure given lung- and heart-toxic chemotherapy
redFlags: B symptoms: unexplained weight loss >10% of body weight over the 6 months before staging, persistent or recurrent fever >38°C in the previous month, or recurrent drenching night sweats in the previous month
Pel-Ebstein fever (cyclic fever with afebrile intervals)
Bulky disease and elevated ESR (>30 with B symptoms; >50 without) marking unfavorable early-stage disease
Fever of unknown origin as a presentation, particularly in older patients with mixed-cellularity HL at an abdominal site
Superior vena cava syndrome from mediastinal involvement (HL is a recognized cause)
harrison.prognosis: cHL is highly curable and a success story of modern oncology, with cure rates now >85%; the overwhelming majority of patients are cured with chemotherapy alone or combined chemotherapy and radiation. Patients are stratified into early-stage (I/II) versus advanced-stage (III/IV) disease. Early-stage patients have a better prognosis overall and are further classified as favorable or unfavorable. In advanced-stage disease, prognosis is best predicted by the International Prognostic Score (IPS), which assigns 1 point each for male sex, age >45 years, stage IV disease, serum albumin <4 g/dL, hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL, white blood cell count >=15,000/uL, and lymphocyte count <600/uL and/or <8% of WBC count; 5-year progression-free survival ranges from 88% (no risk factors) to 62% (four or more factors), though very few patients carry multiple risk factors. NLPHL tends to have a chronic, relapsing course resembling indolent B-cell NHL, with a 15-year nonrelapse survival of 82% for early-stage disease treated with definitive radiotherapy. A major concern is that in some early-stage series more patients died from late treatment complications than from HL itself (p.868-871).
pitfalls: The late age peak in the bimodal distribution may be artifactual, attributable to confusion with similar-appearing entities such as anaplastic large-cell lymphoma and T-cell/histiocyte-rich B-cell lymphoma (p.868).
Bone marrow involvement in cHL is patchy and can be missed on a unilateral marrow biopsy; PET/CT is more accurate (p.869).

Combined-modality therapy in early-stage disease reduces relapse only slightly while increasing late toxicity, with minimal or no improvement in long-term survival; much of the excess risk is attributable to radiotherapy (p.869-870).

NLPHL is biologically distinct from cHL and resembles indolent B-cell NHL; its 'popcorn'/L&H cells are CD30- and CD15-negative (unlike HRS cells), so it should not be managed identically to cHL (p.868, 871).
Alternative regimens (Stanford V, escalated BEACOPP) have not improved survival over standard therapy in early- or advanced-stage disease and are associated with increased toxicity (p.870).
Subdiaphragmatic presentation of cHL is unusual; it is more common in older males (p.869).
harrison.severityClassification: Ann Arbor Staging System: Stage I = single lymph node region or lymphoid structure (e.g., spleen, thymus, Waldeyer's ring); Stage II = two or more node regions on the same side of the diaphragm (mediastinum counts as one site; bilaterally involved hilar nodes constitute stage II); Stage III = node regions/lymphoid structures on both sides of the diaphragm (III1 limited to spleen, splenic hilar, celiac, or portal nodes; III2 adds paraaortic, iliac, or mesenteric nodes); Stage IV = extranodal involvement beyond 'E', more than one extranodal deposit at any location, or any liver/bone marrow involvement. Suffix A = no symptoms; B = unexplained weight loss >10% over 6 months, persistent/recurrent fever >38°C in the previous month, or recurrent drenching night sweats in the previous month; E = localized solitary extralymphatic involvement (excluding liver and bone marrow). Patients are further grouped clinically as early-stage (I/II) versus advanced-stage (III/IV), with early-stage subclassified favorable vs unfavorable and advanced-stage risk-scored by the International Prognostic Score (p.869).
